newsitem.title: CANADA: Parti Quebecois says re-election means referendum.
newsitem.headline: Parti Quebecois says re-election means referendum.

text.p: Quebec's Parti Quebecois government will seek a clear mandate in the next provincial election to hold another referendum on sovereignty, a senior cabinet minister said on Friday.

"We will say very clearly to Quebeckers -- if you re-elect us .. there will be another referendum in the course of the following mandate," Quebec Intergovernmental Affairs Minister Jacques Brassard told reporters.

Elected to power on September 12, 1994, the Parti Quebecois still has three years left in its five-year mandate. Party leader and premier Lucien Bouchard has said previously that he will abide by Quebec law which stipulates that more than one referendum on sovereignty cannot be held during the same government mandate. Bouchard has also said he would like to continue as far as possible with his government's current mandate.
Canadian provincial elections are called at the discretion of the ruling party.

Quebec separatists lost the October 30, 1995 referendum on sovereignty by one percentage point. Since then, tensions between Quebec's French-speaking majority and English-speaking minority have mounted.
Brassard declined to specify how soon after the next provincial election, presuming the Parti Quebecois is returned to power, another referendum would be held.
"It is out of the question to fix a deadline," he said.
Brassard admitted that the Parti Quebecois made a strategic error by having announced after winning the 1994 election that it would hold a referendum on separation within one year.
"I am not telling you that we should not have had a referendum last year, but it is clear that we imposed a constraint on ourselves," he said.
Brassard said the Quebec government's agenda during its current term is to clean up the public finances and put Quebec's lagging economy on the road to recovery.
He acknowledged that the Quebec nationalist fervor had diminished, but warned that it had not disappeared altogether.
"Our mission, until the next referendum, is to make sure that this divided society ceases being divided and that a substantial majority emerges in favor of our (sovereignty) proposal," he said.
